sixtySeconds.whatItDoes: Ultralytics YOLO is a popular Python library and command-line tool for computer vision with YOLO models. It covers object detection, segmentation, classification, pose and oriented bounding boxes, with pretrained models you can use, train on your own data and export for deployment.
sixtySeconds.problem: Building a vision model normally needs a lot of code for data loading, training, evaluation and export. Ultralytics wraps all of that in a few lines of Python or a single yolo command.
whoFor: Developers adding object detection to apps
Students and researchers in computer vision
Teams training custom detectors on their images
Edge and mobile developers exporting to ONNX and other formats
sixtySeconds.whyChoose: Choose it for the easiest path to state-of-the-art YOLO models. It is AGPL-3.0, so commercial products that don't want to open-source their code need an Ultralytics Enterprise License.
requirements: Optional: an NVIDIA GPU for faster training

overview: Ultralytics supports YOLO models from YOLOv3 to the latest YOLO26, with pretrained weights for detection on COCO, segmentation, classification on ImageNet, pose and oriented bounding boxes, plus semantic segmentation and depth models. The README publishes accuracy and speed tables for each.

You can predict, train, validate and export from the yolo command or the Python YOLO class. For example, model.train(data="coco8.yaml", epochs=100) trains on a sample dataset, model.val() evaluates it and model.export(format="onnx") exports it.

Installation is one pip command, with Conda and Docker images also available. Licensing is dual: AGPL-3.0 for open-source use, or an Enterprise License for commercial products without the open-source requirements.

tutorial.title: Train, evaluate and export a YOLO model
tutorial.useCase: Fine-tune YOLO26n on the small COCO8 dataset and export it.

steps.title: Run this script
steps.code:
from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")
train_results = model.train(data="coco8.yaml", epochs=100, imgsz=640, device="cpu")
metrics = model.val()
results = model("path/to/image.jpg")
results[0].show()
path = model.export(format="onnx")

tutorial.expected: A trained model, validation metrics, a displayed prediction and an exported ONNX file.
